titleEn: Type 1 Diabetic With Kussmaul Respirations - Suspected Diabetic Ketoacidosis

patient.name: Ethan Morrison
patient.affectEn: alert and fully oriented but tired, weak and very thirsty; sitting on the edge of his bed leaning forward, breathing deeply and rapidly without any struggle; worried that his pump will not work
patient.speechEn: full sentences between deep breaths; cooperative; answers what he is asked; lets his roommate fill in details he is unsure of

scene.settingEn: 1120 hrs. A small dorm room in a student residence at a college in Prince George. Tidy enough, no hazards, one window open. One patient sitting on the edge of his bed. A bucket beside him holds clear vomit. His roommate is present and worried. An insulin pump clipped to his waistband has a red alarm light flashing; a glucose meter sits on the desk. No PCP car is available in town this morning. University Hospital of Northern BC is 9 minutes away.
hazardsEn: no physical hazards in the room; one window open

bystanders.knowsEn: He has had a sore throat, fever and poor appetite for three days and turned his pump down because he was hardly eating. The pump started alarming yesterday afternoon and he could not fix it; the infusion site on his belly looks red. He started vomiting yesterday evening - more than ten times now. He has been drinking a lot and was up all night urinating, then hardly at all this morning. His meter read 'HI' when he tested last night. The roommate called 911 because his breathing looked weird. Can fetch the pump supplies and the glucose meter if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline, D10W, ondansetron, dimenhydrinate, acetaminophen, ibuprofen

dispatchEn: 1120 hrs. Code 2 to a student residence at a college in Prince George. A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has been vomiting since yesterday and his roommate says he is 'breathing weird'. University Hospital of Northern BC is 9 minutes away. No PCP car is available in town this morning.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: he is awake and answering the phone questions himself. His insulin pump alarm has been going off since last night. He has had flu-like symptoms for three days.
arrivalEn: The roommate meets you at the residence entrance and leads you to a small dorm room. It's tidy enough, there are no hazards, and a window is open. One patient, sitting on the edge of his bed. His roommate stays in the doorway, worried.
firstLookEn: A young man sitting on the edge of his bed, leaning forward, breathing deeply and rapidly but without any obvious struggle. His lips look dry and his eyes look sunken. A bucket beside him holds clear vomit. An insulin pump clipped to his waistband has a red alarm light flashing, and there's a glucose meter on the desk. As you get close you notice a sweet, acetone-like smell on his breath.

primary.locEn: Alert (AVPU = A). Fully oriented to person, place, time and event. Tired.
primary.airwayEn: Patent. Speaking in full sentences between deep breaths. No vomit in the mouth right now, but he has been vomiting repeatedly.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 32, deep and regular. No accessory muscle use. Clear and equal air entry on both sides. He is not struggling to breathe.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 118, present, regular, slightly thready. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: No trauma. Abdomen generally tender without guarding or rebound. No rash. No calf tenderness. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: warm, dry, flushed, with poor turgor and very dry mucous membranes.
primary.skinEn: warm, dry, flushed, poor turgor, very dry mucous membranes

history.ccEn: I've been throwing up since yesterday. My pump kept alarming and I couldn't get it working. I'm so thirsty.

opqrst.oEn: I've been sick for three days - sore throat, fever, not eating. The pump started alarming yesterday afternoon and the throwing up started last night.
opqrst.pEn: Nothing makes it better or worse that I've noticed.
opqrst.qEn: My belly just aches, all over.
opqrst.rEn: It doesn't go anywhere. It's all over my belly.
opqrst.sEn: The belly ache is about a 4 out of 10.
opqrst.tEn: The pump's been broken since yesterday afternoon, so about 18 hours with no insulin. I've thrown up more than ten times since last night.

history.painScoreEn: 4 out of 10 (generalized abdominal ache, no radiation)

sample.sEn: Throwing up, really thirsty, peeing a ton all night and then hardly at all this morning. My belly aches, I'm weak, and my vision's blurry. No chest pain, no headache.
sample.mEn: Just my insulin, through the pump. Nothing else. I turned the pump down a few days ago because I was hardly eating. It's been alarming since yesterday afternoon and I couldn't fix it, so I don't think I've had any insulin since then.
sample.pEn: Type 1 diabetes since I was 11. I've been on the pump for three years. I was in hospital once for ketoacidosis when I was 15.
sample.lEn: Just sips of water this morning. Nothing solid since yesterday morning.
sample.eEn: I've had a sore throat and a fever for three days and I wasn't eating, so I turned my pump down. Yesterday afternoon it started alarming and I couldn't get it working - my roommate says the site looks red. I tested my sugar last night and the meter just said HI.

fe.generalEn: My diabetes was well controlled until this. Three days of sore throat and fever.
fe.cnsEn: I'm weak and tired. I'm not confused. No headache, no weakness on one side.
fe.respiratoryEn: No cough, no pain when I breathe. It feels like I can't get enough air, but it isn't hard work.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart's pounding. No chest pain.
fe.giGuEn: I've thrown up more than ten times. My belly aches all over. I was peeing huge amounts all night and now almost nothing this morning.
fe.integumentaryEn: My skin's really dry. The pump site on my belly is red and sore.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: I'm weak all over and my legs keep cramping.
fe.endocrineEn: Type 1 diabetes. My pump's been broken for about 18 hours.

findings.headNeckEn: Very dry lips and tongue, sunken eyes, sweet acetone odour on the breath, throat red, neck supple.
findings.chestLungsEn: Clear and equal air entry at all six sites. Deep, regular respirations; no accessory muscle use.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft, generally tender without guarding or rebound. Red, tender pump infusion site in the left lower quadrant. Bowel sounds present.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Calf cramping. Pedal pulses present. No swelling and no tenderness suggesting a clot.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Skin tenting on the forearm. Radial pulses present bilaterally. Capillary refill 3 seconds.

resp.character: regular, not laboured, no accessory muscle use

vitalsSets.bgl: HI - above the meter's range (no number is displayed)

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route (or about 16 minutes after set 1): slowly worsening but still no unstable criterion; he has vomited twice more

resp.character: regular, not laboured, no accessory muscle use

vitalsSets.bgl: HI - above the meter's range (no number is displayed)

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: He leans forward and vomits clear fluid again.
He looks up and asks: "Can I please have some water? I'm so thirsty."

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan equipment: blood glucose meter, oxygen, suction, thermometer, emesis bags, blankets and the stretcher
Recognize the pattern from dispatch: a type 1 diabetic with an insulin delivery failure, days of illness and vomiting, and abnormal breathing - suspect ketoacidosis before you walk in
Plan to bring the insulin pump and his glucose log with the patient - the receiving team needs to know how long insulin delivery has failed
triggers: plan to bring the insulin pump
how long the pump has failed

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (none), environment, nature of illness (three days of illness with vomiting in a type 1 diabetic), people (one patient plus a roommate who can give collateral history) and resources (no PCP available - this is an EMR-only call)
Don gloves and eye protection - he is actively vomiting
First look: young man, alert, deep rapid unlaboured breathing, dry lips, sunken eyes, a flashing pump alarm - and note the sweet acetone smell on his breath
Assess LOC / AVPU: alert and fully oriented, GCS 15 - and state that any drop from this is the finding that would change everything
triggers: any drop in LOC changes everything

expected.actionEn: Assess the airway; keep suction beside him because he is vomiting repeatedly
triggers: he's talking so his airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing and interpret it correctly: 32 per minute, deep, regular, no accessory muscle use, clear air entry - Kussmaul respiration compensating for acidosis, NOT respiratory distress and NOT a reason for assisted ventilation
Assess circulation: radial pulse 118, present and slightly thready with poor skin turgor - volume depletion from osmotic diuresis and vomiting
Perform the rapid body survey including a gentle abdominal examination - abdominal pain is common in ketoacidosis but a surgical abdomen must not be assumed away
Note the skin: warm, dry, flushed, poor turgor, very dry mucous membranes

Reason the oxygen decision out loud: his SpO2 is 98% and his tachypnea is compensatory, not hypoxic, so oxygen is titrated only to keep SpO2 at or above 94% and is not required now - reassess with every set of vitals
triggers: oxygen only if he drops below 94

expected.actionEn: Position of comfort, sitting or semi-reclined with an emesis bag and suction, ready to move him lateral if his LOC falls
Correctly categorize as non-RTC and justify it against the unstable criteria one by one
State the findings that would upgrade him immediately: falling LOC, systolic below 90, absent radial pulses, or slowing respirations from fatigue
triggers: if he loses his radial pulses

expected.actionEn: Ready for transport within 30 minutes without dawdling, and take the insulin pump and glucose meter with the patient
triggers: pump and meter come with us

expected.actionEn: Establish the chief complaint: vomiting, thirst and abnormal breathing in a type 1 diabetic with a failed insulin pump
Take the HxC/C: how long insulin delivery has been interrupted, the precipitating illness, vomiting frequency, thirst, urine output overnight and today, and the last glucose reading
triggers: when did the pump stop working
how many times have you vomited
how long have you been sick

expected.actionEn: Score the abdominal pain and characterize it - abdominal pain is common in ketoacidosis but must still be described properly
triggers: how bad is the belly pain

expected.actionEn: Past medical history, including the previous ketoacidosis admission
triggers: been in hospital for this before
how long have you been diabetic

expected.actionEn: Medications - insulin by pump only, and when the last effective dose was actually delivered
Allergies
Last oral intake
GCS with all three components stated separately
Blood pressure by auscultation - 104/68 is above the hypotension threshold but low for a 19-year-old and must be trended
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality
Respiratory rate, depth and character with both lung fields auscultated, and describe the pattern as deep and regular rather than laboured
Skin assessed hands-on including turgor and mucous membranes
Pupils - size, equality and reaction
SpO2 recorded - and not used as evidence that the breathing is fine, because a normal saturation does not exclude a severe metabolic acidosis
Blood glucose measured and documented honestly as above the meter's range
Temperature - indicated because an infection appears to have precipitated this episode
FE - General health
FE - CNS (no confusion yet - this is the system to watch)
FE - Respiratory (air hunger without laboured breathing is the classic ketoacidosis description)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (the swing from polyuria overnight to almost no urine this morning quantifies the volume loss)
FE - Integumentary (inspect the pump infusion site - a red tender site explains the insulin failure)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine (how long insulin delivery has been interrupted is the key number)
triggers: how long has the pump been off

expected.actionEn: FE - EENT
Head and neck examined, including mucous membranes and the breath odour
Chest auscultated at all six sites to confirm the lungs are clear - the tachypnea is metabolic, not pulmonary
Abdomen examined in four quadrants, including inspection of the pump infusion site
Back examined
Upper extremities with skin turgor and capillary refill documented as dehydration markers
Lower extremities with pedal pulses documented

Measure the blood glucose and correctly withhold oral glucose and glucagon with a reading above the meter's range - giving glucose to a hyperglycemic patient is initiating a protocol without indications
triggers: his sugar is high so no glucose
BGL is HI so no glucose

expected.actionEn: Rule out and verbalize the analgesia contraindications before considering anything for the abdominal pain: he cannot retain oral medication while vomiting, and Entonox is cautioned in shock and abdominal distension
triggers: he can't keep oral meds down

expected.actionEn: Evaluate for stroke signs and symptoms as the Diabetic Emergencies protocol requires
Airway management: emesis bag and suction within reach, positioned upright or lateral, with a stated plan to go fully lateral if the LOC falls
Verbalize that intravenous fluid and insulin are outside EMR scope and are the reason he is going to hospital now rather than later
triggers: IV fluids are outside my scope
he needs IV fluids and insulin

expected.actionEn: Bring the insulin pump, the infusion set and the glucose meter with the patient and document the infusion site appearance
triggers: bring the pump, infusion set and meter

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs and interventions after each move and at regular intervals
Second full set of vitals within 15 minutes and interpret the trend out loud as slow worsening that still does not meet unstable criteria
State the decompensation trigger: if the deep respirations slow as he tires, that is respiratory failure and assisted ventilation with a BVM begins immediately
Protect the airway through repeated vomiting, with suction in hand and a plan to go lateral if the LOC falls
triggers: roll him lateral if he vomits

expected.actionEn: Notify the receiving hospital of a suspected ketoacidosis so intravenous fluid and insulin can be prepared
Complete verbal hand-off including the duration of insulin interruption, the glucose reading and the respiratory pattern
Accurate PCR completed within 5 minutes, documenting the glucose as above meter range rather than a guessed number

specialEvents.descriptionEn: the candidate actually administers oral glucose / glucose gel, glucagon or D10W to this patient (also report the drug event). Saying that glucose or glucagon is withheld, not indicated, cannot be given or is not needed is NOT this event.

the candidate starts assisted ventilations (BVM, pocket mask, assisting breaths, positive pressure) while the patient is alert and breathing deeply and regularly on his own. Stating a plan to ventilate IF his breathing slows or he tires is NOT this event.
the candidate gives the patient water or any other oral fluid to drink, or tells him he can drink
a PCP candidate actually gives acetaminophen or ibuprofen by mouth to this patient, who has vomited more than ten times (also report the drug event)

the candidate actually administers Entonox to this patient (cautioned in shock and abdominal distension; nausea and vomiting are adverse effects); also report drug:entonox. Saying Entonox is withheld or cautioned is NOT this event.
an EMR candidate actually starts an IV, runs a fluid bolus, or gives ondansetron, dimenhydrinate, acetaminophen, ibuprofen or D10W. Saying these are outside EMR scope is NOT this event.
the candidate applies high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather while the SpO2 is 98% on room air, without a stated rationale
a PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL or onto the next bag without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between
the candidate evaluates for stroke signs and symptoms (e.g. FAST-VAN: facial droop, arm drift, speech, vision, neglect), as the Diabetic Emergencies protocol requires

drugs.doseEn: 15 g PO to the oral mucosa - NOT indicated here: the protocol corrects hypoglycemia (BGL below 4.0 mmol/L) and this meter reads HI. Report drug:oral-glucose only if the candidate actually gives it.
IM 0.5-1 mg or IN 3 mg for hypoglycemia - NOT indicated here (BGL reads HI). Report drug:glucagon only if the candidate actually gives it.
10-25 g IV (100-250 mL of 10%) for confirmed hypoglycemia - NOT indicated here (BGL reads HI)
self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this call: cautioned in shock and abdominal distension, and nausea and vomiting are adverse effects in a patient vomiting repeatedly
500-1,000 mg PO - WITHHELD: he cannot retain oral medication after vomiting more than ten times
300-400 mg PO - WITHHELD: he cannot retain oral medication after vomiting more than ten times
PCP: 20 mL/kg IV bolus to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing every 500 mL, for the volume depletion
PCP may consider 4 mg PO (adult) for moderate to severe nausea and vomiting
PCP may consider 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg, IV diluted over 2 minutes or IM

deduct.errorEn: Initiated protocol without proper indications (e.g. patient is not DLOC)
Does not sufficiently assess the patient to determine appropriate treatment (e.g. only assessing LOC to determine the need for Narcan)
Ventilates a patient when not required

Performs an act that could aggravate the patient's condition or injury that is not already captured in the major performance criteria (e.g. excessively bumping a fractured leg which causes gross movement and pain)
Does not rule out all the contraindications, potentially detrimental to patient care
Does not rule out all the cautions of a medication
Initiated protocol without proper indications (e.g. patient is not DLOC)
Applies oxygen but it is applied with minor deficiencies
Does not perform an act that was required based on patient presentation that is not detrimental to patient care
Performs the protocol with isolated error with potential to be detrimental to patient care

examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: He is breathing deeply and rapidly, but regularly and without any struggle: no accessory muscle use.

trackNotes.emrEn: The EMR contribution is judgement rather than intervention: measure the glucose and correctly do nothing with it, read the deep breathing as compensation rather than distress, keep the airway clear through repeated vomiting, call it non-RTC while still moving with purpose, withhold oral glucose, glucagon, oral fluids and analgesia with the reasons stated, evaluate for stroke signs, take the pump and meter along, and hand over a precise history. IV fluid and insulin are outside EMR scope. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry and vascular access en route with a fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L, reassessed every 500 mL; ondansetron or dimenhydrinate may be considered for the vomiting. Oral analgesia is withheld (he cannot retain it). Insulin is not carried at either level.

sourcePages: Scenario emd-07 (data/practical/emr-medical-1.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions (glucose, fluid and analgesia traps), ongoing, handoff, critical pitfalls. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (none met - non-RTC); p.48 Nausea - Vomiting PCP (suction ready, position, dimenhydrinate or ondansetron, fluid bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 litres reassessing every 500 mL); p.50 Oxygen Administration (titrate to SpO2 94% if not SOB or in shock); p.57 Diabetic Emergencies (baseline vitals including blood glucose, evaluate for stroke signs and symptoms, correct hypoglycemia BGL < 4.0 mmol/L with glucose gel; EMR glucagon for insufficient mentation; PCP D10W 10-25 g, glucagon if no IV access); p.58 Acetaminophen (500-1,000 mg PO); p.63 Dimenhydrinate (1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg); p.65 Entonox (cautions: shock, abdominal distention; adverse effects nausea and vomiting); p.67 Glucagon (indication hypoglycemia; IM 0.5-1 mg, IN 3 mg); p.68 Ibuprofen (300-400 mg PO); p.75 Ondansetron (4 mg PO); p.76 Oral Glucose (15 g PO).
